stories.event: A son-in-law passed by the entrance of his father-in-law's house.
stories.turn: There were rumors of intimacy between him and his mother-in-law, so passing by fed the suspicion.
stories.outcome: Rav Sheshet flogged him.
stories.summary: A certain son-in-law walked past the door of his father-in-law's house. Because there were rumors linking him with his mother-in-law, Rav Sheshet had him flogged for it.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with a myrtle mat
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman with a mat of myrtle branches.
stories.turn: Bystanders objected that the mat was worth less than a peruta, so he declared she should be betrothed with the four dinars wrapped inside; she took it and stayed silent.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that silence after the money is given means nothing, so the betrothal did not take effect.
stories.summary: A man tried to betroth a woman with a myrtle mat. When people pointed out it was worth less than a peruta, he said she should be betrothed with the four dinars inside it. She took the mat and said nothing, and Rava ruled her silence after receiving the money was meaningless.

stories.actor: A purchaser of land and a creditor
stories.event: The purchaser took one hundred dinars to the creditor and offered him either the tract or the money to give up his claim.
stories.turn: The question was whether the creditor could refuse the cash and insist on the land.
stories.outcome: Abaye held the creditor suffers no loss, since he lent a hundred and receives a hundred, so he must accept.
stories.summary: A purchaser went to a creditor with one hundred dinars and told him to accept the tract at that value or take the money and give up his claim. Rav Yosef compared the case to the mishna about orphans, but Abaye answered that the creditor loses nothing, getting back exactly what he lent.

stories.event: A creditor seized a small field the dead debtor left; the orphans paid him fifty dinars to redeem it, and he seized it again for the rest of the debt.
stories.turn: The orphans complained to Abaye.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled their payment was a mitzva of settling their father's debt but did not lift the lien, so the second seizure was lawful.
stories.summary: A man died owing one hundred dinars and left a field worth fifty. The creditor seized it, the orphans paid fifty to redeem it, and then the creditor seized it again. Abaye told the orphans they had fulfilled the mitzva of paying their father's debt, but the creditor was within his rights.

stories.actor: A man who sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract
stories.event: A man sold the future rights to his mother's ketubba, saying he would not repay if his mother objected.
stories.turn: His mother died without objecting, but he himself then contested the sale.
stories.outcome: Rami bar Hama thought he stood in his mother's place, but Rava ruled he had surely guaranteed the sale against his own objections.
stories.summary: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract, disclaiming responsibility if she objected. She died without objecting, and he then tried to contest the sale himself. Rava rejected him: he may not have guaranteed against his mother, but he certainly guaranteed against himself.

stories.event: Redeemed captive women were lodged in Rav Amram's attic with the ladder removed; seeing one's beauty, he lifted a ladder ten men could not and began to climb.
stories.turn: Halfway up he braced himself and cried 'Fire in Amram's house!', bringing the Sages, who said he had shamed them.
stories.outcome: He said shame in this world beats shame in the next, made his evil inclination leave him as a pillar of fire, and declared himself stronger than it.
stories.summary: Captive women were brought to Rav Amram's house and the ladder to their attic was taken away. Overcome by desire for one of them, he lifted a huge ladder by himself and started up, but halfway he stopped and shouted that there was a fire, so people would come. When the Sages said he had embarrassed them, he answered that it was better than shame in the World-to-Come. He then forced his evil inclination out of himself as a pillar of fire.

stories.event: Rabbi Meir, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman across a river and began crossing on a rope bridge.
stories.turn: Halfway across, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan told him that only the heavenly warning to protect Rabbi Meir and his Torah had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to scoff at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman across a river, and he started across a rope bridge to reach her. Halfway over, Satan let him go and said that if heaven had not warned 'Be careful with Rabbi Meir,' he would have ruined him.

stories.event: Rabbi Akiva, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman atop a palm tree and began climbing.
stories.turn: Halfway up, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said only the heavenly warning about Rabbi Akiva had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva also scoffed at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree and he began climbing toward her. Halfway up, Satan released him, saying heaven's protection was all that saved him.

stories.event: Peleimu, who daily said 'An arrow in Satan's eye', was visited on Yom Kippur eve by Satan disguised as a repulsive pauper, who demanded to come in and sit at the table.
stories.turn: Satan spat into a cup, pretended to die, and people cried that Peleimu had killed a man, so he fled and hid in the bathroom.
stories.outcome: Satan revealed himself and told Peleimu to say instead 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan'.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to taunt Satan every day. On the eve of Yom Kippur Satan came as a diseased beggar, pushed his way inside and to the table, behaved disgustingly, spat in a cup and then collapsed as if dead. People accused Peleimu of murder and he hid in the bathroom. Satan then revealed himself and told him to stop taunting and say 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan' instead.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents
stories.event: Heirs demanded a bag of documents deposited with a woman, and she claimed she had seized it from the deceased in his lifetime for a debt.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman asked for witnesses that the deceased had demanded it from her while alive, and she had none.
stories.outcome: He ruled it was a seizure after death, which is ineffective.
stories.summary: A woman held a bag of documents that heirs claimed. She said she had seized it from the dead man during his life to cover a debt. Rav Nahman asked whether she had witnesses that he had demanded it and she refused; she had none, so he ruled her seizure counted as after death and was void.

stories.actor: Rava and the daughter of Rav Hisda
stories.event: A woman was obligated to take an oath in Rava's court.
stories.turn: Rava's wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, told him the woman was suspected of false oaths.
stories.outcome: Rava transferred the oath to the opposing party.
stories.summary: A woman had to swear an oath in Rava's court. His wife told him she knew the woman to be untrustworthy with oaths, so Rava reversed the oath onto the other side.

stories.event: A document came before Rava and Rav Pappa testified that it had been paid.
stories.turn: Rava refused to rely on a lone witness, and Rav Adda bar Mattana objected that he had relied on Rav Hisda's daughter.
stories.outcome: Rava answered that he knew her to be truthful with certainty but not Rav Pappa.
stories.summary: While Rav Pappa and Rav Adda bar Mattana sat before Rava, a document was brought and Rav Pappa said he knew it was paid. Rava asked whether anyone else knew, and on hearing no, said one witness is nothing. When Rav Adda asked why Rav Pappa was worth less than Rav Hisda's daughter, Rava said he was certain of her honesty but not of Rav Pappa's.

stories.actor: A woman in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court
stories.event: A woman was required to take an oath, and her opponent asked that she swear publicly in town in hope she would be ashamed and admit.
stories.turn: She demanded a document of rights first so she would be paid once she swore.
stories.outcome: Rav Beivai bar Abaye ordered the document written for her.
stories.summary: In Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court a woman owed an oath, and the other litigant asked that she take it in town where shame might make her confess. She agreed only if they first wrote her a document guaranteeing payment after she swore, and Rav Beivai told them to write it.

stories.event: Homa came before Rava asking for food and wine from Abaye's estate; when he doubted Abaye drank wine, she gestured at the size of his cups and her arm was uncovered.
stories.turn: Her beauty lit up the court; Rava went home and asked his wife for intimacy, and she learned Homa had been in court.
stories.outcome: Rav Hisda's daughter chased Homa out of Mehoza, beating her with a chest lock and accusing her of killing three husbands and coming for a fourth.
stories.summary: After Abaye died, his widow Homa asked Rava to award her food and then wine. When Rava said Abaye did not drink wine, she showed with her arms how big his cups were and her bare arm dazzled the court. Rava went home stirred, and his wife, learning who had been in court, chased Homa out of the city with blows, accusing her of having already killed three husbands.

stories.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava
stories.event: She asked Rav Nehemya son of Rav Yosef to award her food and then wine.
stories.turn: He granted the wine as well.
stories.outcome: He explained that the people of Mehoza drink wine, so she was entitled to it.
stories.summary: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rava came before Rav Nehemya asking for food, then wine. He granted both, saying that the people of Mehoza customarily drink wine.

stories.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of D'vil
stories.event: She asked Rav Yosef for food, wine, and then silk garments.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef asked why she needed silk.
stories.outcome: She answered: for you, your friends and your friends' friends, so she would not be shamed before them.
stories.summary: A widow came to Rav Yosef and was granted food and wine, then asked for silk clothes. When he asked why, she said she needed them for appearing before him and his colleagues and their colleagues.

stories.actor: Yehuda bar Mareimar, Rav Pappa and Abba of Sura
stories.event: Rav Pappa went to write the marriage contract for his son's bride, daughter of Abba of Sura, and pressed Yehuda bar Mareimar, who escorted him, to enter the house.
stories.turn: Yehuda feared his presence would pressure Abba of Sura; he entered and sat silent, so Abba, thinking him angry, wrote over all his property as dowry.
stories.outcome: Yehuda said he disliked even that, and when Abba offered to retract, told him not to make himself a man who goes back on his word.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa went to arrange the marriage contract for his son with the family of Abba of Sura, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to honor him but would not enter. Rav Pappa argued with him and finally forced him in. Yehuda sat silently, and Abba of Sura, thinking he was angry, signed away everything he owned as dowry. Yehuda then said he disapproved even of that, but when Abba offered to retract, told him he should not become someone who goes back on his word.

stories.event: Avimi always ran to open the door for his father; one day his father asked for water and fell asleep before Avimi returned.
stories.turn: Avimi stood bent over him until he woke.
stories.outcome: As a reward he succeeded in expounding the psalm 'A song of Asaph'.
stories.summary: Though himself ordained with five ordained sons, Avimi would run to open the door for his father, Rabbi Abbahu. Once his father asked for water and dozed off before he brought it, so Avimi stood bent over him until he woke. In reward, heaven helped him expound Psalm 79.

stories.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could step on him to get into and out of bed, and he boasted about it in the study hall.
stories.turn: The Sages told him he had not reached even half of the honor due her.
stories.outcome: They asked whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea before him without his shaming her.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon let his mother climb on him to get into and out of bed, and he praised himself for it in the study hall. The Sages deflated him: he had not done half the mitzva unless she had thrown his money into the sea and he still did not shame her.

stories.event: Rav Asi's elderly mother kept making demands, finally asking for a husband as handsome as he was.
stories.turn: Realizing she was senile, he left for Eretz Yisrael, then heard she was following him and asked Rabbi Yohanan whether he could leave the Land to meet her.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he did not know, and when Asi came back, saw he was determined and blessed him to return in peace.
stories.summary: Rav Asi's aged mother asked for jewelry, which he made, then a husband, then one as handsome as him. Seeing she was beyond satisfying, he moved to Eretz Yisrael. Hearing she was coming after him, he asked Rabbi Yohanan if he could leave the Land to meet his mother; Rabbi Yohanan would not decide and finally said, 'May God bring you back in peace.'

stories.actor: A man's daughter and his heirs
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter, but the orphans divided the estate without giving her one.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef compared it to the mishna where each party can deflect the claim.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled the tree is in all their possession, so they must give her a palm tree and redivide the estate.
stories.summary: A man left instructions that his daughter get a palm tree, but the heirs split the property and gave her none. Rav Yosef thought each heir could say it was not in his share, but Abaye disagreed: they jointly owed her the tree, so they must give it and divide the estate again.

stories.actor: A daughter left 'a palm tree' and Rav Ashi
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter but died owning only two half-shares of palm trees, which the heirs offered her.
stories.turn: Rav Ashi questioned whether two halves count as 'a palm tree'.
stories.outcome: Rav Mordekhai reported in Rava's name that people do call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs' offer stood.
stories.summary: Another man promised his daughter a palm tree but left only two half-trees. The heirs wanted to give her the two halves, and Rav Ashi wondered whether that fulfilled the bequest. Rav Mordekhai told him that, according to Rava, two halves are commonly called a palm tree.

stories.event: He expounded every 'et' in the Torah until he reached 'You shall fear (et) the Lord your God' and withdrew.
stories.turn: His students asked what would become of all his previous expositions.
stories.outcome: He said he was rewarded for withdrawing as for expounding; later Rabbi Akiva interpreted that 'et' to include Torah scholars.
stories.summary: Shimon HaAmasoni used to derive laws from every occurrence of the word 'et'. When he reached the verse about fearing God, he could not think what else could be feared alongside God and gave up the method. His students asked about his earlier teachings, and he said he was rewarded for stopping as he had been for expounding; Rabbi Akiva later explained that verse as including Torah scholars.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents
stories.event: Heirs demanded a bag of documents deposited with a woman, and she claimed she had seized it from the deceased in his lifetime for a debt.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman asked for witnesses that the deceased had demanded it from her while alive, and she had none.
stories.outcome: He ruled it was a seizure after death, which is ineffective.
stories.summary: A woman held a bag of documents the heirs claimed, saying she had seized it from the dead man while he lived. Rav Nahman asked for witnesses that he had demanded it back and she refused; she had none, so he ruled the seizure was after death and void.

stories.actor: Rava and the daughter of Rav Hisda
stories.event: A woman was obligated to take an oath in Rava's court.
stories.turn: Rava's wife told him the woman was suspected of false oaths.
stories.outcome: Rava transferred the oath to the opposing party.
stories.summary: A woman had to take an oath in Rava's court. His wife, Rav Hisda's daughter, told him the woman could not be trusted with oaths, so Rava reversed the oath onto the other litigant.

stories.event: A document came before Rava and Rav Pappa testified that it had been paid.
stories.turn: Rava refused to rely on a lone witness, and Rav Adda bar Mattana objected that he had relied on Rav Hisda's daughter.
stories.outcome: Rava answered that he knew her to be truthful with certainty but not Rav Pappa.
stories.summary: A document was brought before Rava and Rav Pappa said he knew it had been paid. Rava said one witness is nothing. Rav Adda bar Mattana asked why Rav Pappa was not trusted like Rav Hisda's daughter, and Rava replied that he was certain of her honesty but not of his.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira, Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Three Sages visiting a place were served a peach as big as a five-se'a stewpot and shared it among themselves, the public and their animals.
stories.turn: A year later Rabbi Elazar came there and was served a peach small enough to hold in one hand.
stories.outcome: He cited the verse that a fruitful land turns to salt waste for the wickedness of its inhabitants.
stories.summary: Three Sages visited a place and were brought an enormous peach, which fed them, passersby and their animals. The next year Rabbi Elazar came and was given a peach that fit in his hand. He quoted the verse blaming the shrinking of the land's fruit on the sins of its people.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw grape clusters in Gavla as big as calves and cried to the earth to withhold its fruit from the gentiles ruling them.
stories.turn: The next year Rabbi Hiyya found the clusters only as big as goats.
stories.outcome: When he remarked on them, the locals told him to go away and not do what his colleague had done.
stories.summary: In Gavla, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi mistook giant grape clusters for calves and then called on the land to stop producing such fruit for the gentiles who ruled Israel. A year later the clusters had shrunk to the size of goats. When Rabbi Hiyya commented on them, the locals sent him off, afraid he would curse them as his colleague had.

stories.actor: Two men drinking wine in Babylonia
stories.event: One handed the other a cup of wine and said, 'Let your daughter be betrothed to my son.'
stories.turn: The question was whether the son's possible consent or agency made it a betrothal.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled there is no concern that the son agreed, and rejected the suggestions that the son appointed or prompted his father.
stories.summary: Two men drinking under the poplars in Babylonia: one gave the other a cup of wine as betrothal of his friend's daughter to his own son. Ravina ruled that we do not assume the son agreed to it, and answered the Sages' objections that the son might have made his father his agent or hinted his wish.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed a girl with vegetables
stories.event: A man betrothed a minor girl without her father's consent using a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace.
stories.turn: The question was whether the father might have approved.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled that because it was done degradingly, there is no concern that the father approved.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a young girl with a bunch of vegetables in the market, without her father. Ravina ruled that even those who worry the father may have approved would not worry here, because the act was degrading.

stories.actor: A father, a mother, and the father's relative
stories.event: Parents disputed whom their minor daughter would marry; the mother pressed until the father agreed to her relative.
stories.turn: While they were eating the betrothal feast, the father's relative climbed onto the roof and betrothed her himself.
stories.outcome: Abaye and Rava held the father did not want that betrothal, because he would keep his word and would not waste the feast.
stories.summary: A father wanted his daughter to marry his relative, the mother wanted hers, and she pressed until he gave in. During the festive meal, the father's relative went up to the roof and betrothed the girl. Abaye and Rava reasoned that the father would not have wanted this, since he had given his word and had gone to the trouble of a feast.

stories.event: Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged by a pig.
stories.turn: He exclaimed that a mouth that produced pearls should lick dust.
stories.outcome: He went out and sinned.
stories.summary: One account of Elisha ben Avuya's apostasy: he saw the tongue of the executed scholar Hutzpit dragged through the street by a pig. Asking how a mouth that spoke pearls could lick dirt, he went out and abandoned the Torah.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi; he made himself covered in boils by an incantation, but she healed him by magic.
stories.turn: He fled and hid in a demon-infested bathhouse where people were harmed even in daylight.
stories.outcome: He survived the night guarded by two angelic soldiers, and the Sages explained the miracle as reward for resisting forbidden intercourse.
stories.summary: A noblewoman pursued Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. He made himself repulsive with boils, but she cured him with sorcery, so he ran and hid in a deadly haunted bathhouse. The next day he told the Sages two of the emperor's guards had protected him all night, and they said it was a miracle for escaping sin.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok; he pleaded weakness and asked for food, and she began roasting non-kosher food in an oven.
stories.turn: He climbed into the oven, saying one who does this act falls into this fire.
stories.outcome: She said that had she known how serious it was to him she would not have tormented him.
stories.summary: When a noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok, he stalled by asking for food, and she lit the oven to cook non-kosher meat. He climbed into the oven himself, explaining that whoever commits this sin falls into fire. Shaken, she said she would not have troubled him had she known.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rav Kahana, who sold baskets; he said he would go adorn himself and instead threw himself off the roof.
stories.turn: Elijah came and caught him, complaining he had had to travel four hundred parasangs.
stories.outcome: Rav Kahana blamed his poverty, and Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.
stories.summary: Rav Kahana sold baskets, and a noblewoman propositioned him. Pretending to go prepare himself, he jumped from the roof, but Elijah caught him and grumbled about the long trip. When Rav Kahana said his poverty had put him in that position, Elijah gave him a basket full of money.

stories.event: Rav Sheshet awarded the property to Rami bar Hama and Rav Nahman awarded it to his brother Mar Ukva; Rav Sheshet challenged Rav Nahman.
stories.turn: Rav Sheshet's reason, that one deed came first, was refuted because hours are not written outside Jerusalem; Rav Nahman cited judges' discretion.
stories.outcome: When Rav Sheshet claimed discretion too, Rav Nahman replied that he was the judge, not Rav Sheshet, and that Sheshet had not ruled on that basis.
stories.summary: The brothers Rami bar Hama and Mar Ukva each got a ruling in his favor, one from Rav Sheshet and one from Rav Nahman. Rav Sheshet confronted Rav Nahman, who dismissed Sheshet's reasoning about which deed was earlier and said he had used judicial discretion. When Rav Sheshet claimed the same, Rav Nahman said that he, not Sheshet, was the appointed judge, and that Sheshet had not ruled on that ground anyway.

stories.actor: Two deed holders before Rav Yosef
stories.event: Two deeds for the same land came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one just 'Nisan', and he awarded it to the dated one.
stories.turn: The loser protested; Rav Yosef said his deed could be from the 29th, so he asked for authorization to repossess from purchasers after Iyyar.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef refused, since those purchasers could say his deed was from the first of Nisan and the field was rightfully his.
stories.summary: Two men held deeds to one field, one dated the fifth of Nisan and the other only 'Nisan'. Rav Yosef gave the field to the man with the exact date, telling the other he must assume the latest date. When the loser asked for a document to collect from the seller's later sales, Rav Yosef refused, because those buyers could say his deed was earliest and the field was really his.

stories.actor: Rav Minyumi son of Rav Nihumi and Ameimar
stories.event: A woman came before Ameimar asking for a tenth of her father's estate for her dowry, and her brothers told her that if they had money they would pay her off in cash.
stories.turn: Ameimar stayed silent and did not object.
stories.outcome: Rav Minyumi took his silence to show Ameimar had retracted and held her a creditor who can be paid in cash.
stories.summary: Rav Minyumi was standing before Ameimar when a woman asked for a tenth of her father's estate. Her brothers said they would pay her in cash if they had it, and Ameimar said nothing. From that silence Rav Minyumi concluded Ameimar now held a daughter to be a creditor rather than an heir.

stories.event: Dama ben Netina sat among Roman nobles in a golden cloak when his mother came, tore it off, struck his head and spat in his face.
stories.turn: He was publicly humiliated by her.
stories.outcome: He did not shame her in return.
stories.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Dama ben Netina was once sitting among the nobles of Rome in a gold-embroidered cloak when his mother tore it off him, hit him on the head and spat in his face. Even so, he did not embarrass her.

stories.event: Avimi always ran to open the door for his father; one day his father asked for water and fell asleep before Avimi returned.
stories.turn: Avimi stood bent over him until he woke.
stories.outcome: As a reward he succeeded in expounding the psalm 'A song of Asaph'.
stories.summary: Avimi, though ordained and with ordained sons, would run to open the door for his father, Rabbi Abbahu. Once his father asked for water and fell asleep, and Avimi stood bent over him until he woke. As a reward he managed to expound Psalm 79.

stories.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could step on him to get into and out of bed, and boasted of it in the study hall.
stories.turn: The Sages told him he had not reached half the honor due her.
stories.outcome: They asked whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea without his shaming her.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon let his mother use him as a step into and out of bed and praised himself for it. The Sages told him he had not done half his duty unless she had thrown his purse into the sea in front of him and he still did not embarrass her.

stories.event: Redeemed captive women were lodged in Rav Amram's attic with the ladder removed; seeing one's beauty, he lifted a ladder ten men could not and began to climb.
stories.turn: Halfway up he braced himself and cried 'Fire in Amram's house!', bringing the Sages, who said he had shamed them.
stories.outcome: He said shame in this world beats shame in the next, made his evil inclination leave as a pillar of fire, and declared himself stronger than it.
stories.summary: Captive women were housed in Rav Amram's attic with the ladder removed. Desiring one of them, he lifted an enormous ladder alone and began to climb, but halfway he stopped and shouted 'fire' to bring people. When the Sages complained of the embarrassment, he said it was better than shame in the World-to-Come, then drove out his evil inclination like a pillar of fire.

stories.event: Rabbi Meir, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman across a river and began crossing on a rope bridge.
stories.turn: Halfway across, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said only heaven's warning to protect Rabbi Meir had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to mock sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman on the far bank, and he started across on a rope bridge. Halfway, Satan let him go, saying heaven's protection alone had spared him.

stories.event: Rabbi Akiva, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman atop a palm tree and began climbing.
stories.turn: Halfway up, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said only heaven's warning about Rabbi Akiva had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva also mocked sinners. Satan appeared as a woman at the top of a palm tree and he began to climb. Halfway up Satan released him, saying heaven's warning was all that protected him.

stories.event: Peleimu, who daily said 'An arrow in Satan's eye', was visited on Yom Kippur eve by Satan disguised as a pauper who demanded to come in and sit at the table.
stories.turn: The pauper sat covered with boils and behaved repulsively at the table.
stories.outcome: The window ends as Peleimu begins to rebuke him.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to taunt Satan daily. On the eve of Yom Kippur Satan came to his door as a beggar, insisted on coming in and then on sitting at the table, and sat there covered in sores, acting disgustingly. Peleimu began to speak to him as the window ends.

stories.actor: People who found a fox in a turnip
stories.event: A fox nested inside a turnip.
stories.turn: They weighed the turnip.
stories.outcome: It weighed sixty litra by the Tzippori measure.
stories.summary: As evidence of how large produce can grow, the Sages cite an incident in which a fox made its nest inside a turnip. When the turnip was weighed, it came to sixty litra.

stories.event: A man inherited three mustard stalks, and one of them broke.
stories.turn: Nine kav of mustard were found on that single stalk.
stories.outcome: Its wood was used to roof a potters' booth.
stories.summary: Rav Yosei reported an incident in Shihin: a man's father left him three mustard stalks, and when one broke it held nine kav of mustard seed. Its wood was enough to roof a craftsmen's hut.

stories.event: Mar Ukva secretly left four dinars daily for a poor neighbor; one day the poor man came out to see who it was while Mar Ukva and his wife were at the door.
stories.turn: They fled into a still-hot furnace, where Mar Ukva's feet burned but his wife's did not, and he was distressed.
stories.outcome: She explained that her charity of ready food was more immediate than his money.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva used to slip four dinars through a poor neighbor's door each day. One day the man came out to catch his benefactor, so Mar Ukva and his wife ran and hid in a hot furnace. His feet were burning while hers were not, and when he was upset, she told him it was because she gave food directly at home, which helps the poor more quickly.

stories.event: Mar Ukva sent four hundred dinars to a poor neighbor on Yom Kippur eve by his son.
stories.turn: The son returned saying the man did not need it, since he saw old wine sprinkled for him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva said he was so pampered he needed more, and doubled the gift.
stories.summary: Every Yom Kippur eve Mar Ukva sent a poor man four hundred dinars. Once his son brought it and came back saying the man was so well off they poured old wine on the floor for him. Mar Ukva concluded the man was used to luxury and sent him double.

stories.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records and saw he had given seven thousand gold dinars.
stories.turn: He declared his provisions light for a long journey.
stories.outcome: He gave away half of his remaining wealth.
stories.summary: As Mar Ukva lay dying he asked to see his charity accounts, which showed seven thousand gold dinars. Saying this was too little provision for the long road ahead, he gave away half his fortune.

stories.event: Rabbi Hanina sent four dinars every Shabbat eve to a pauper; one day he sent them with his wife.
stories.turn: She came back saying the man did not need it, having heard them ask him what he dines on.
stories.outcome: The window ends before the outcome.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send a poor man four dinars each Friday. Once his wife delivered it and returned saying he did not need charity, since she had overheard them asking what he eats; the story continues past the window.

stories.event: Seeing his son's studies with Abaye were weak, Rav Aha bar Ya'akov went to study himself; Abaye had the townspeople deny him lodging so he would sleep in the study hall haunted by a demon.
stories.turn: The demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent, and with each bow of his prayer one head fell off.
stories.outcome: The demon was killed, and the next day he told them that without a miracle they would have endangered him.
stories.summary: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov sent his son to Abaye, but seeing the son was not sharp, decided to go study himself. Abaye told the town not to host him, hoping he would spend the night in the demon-haunted study hall and a miracle would happen. The demon came as a seven-headed serpent, and each bow of his prayer cut off a head. In the morning he told them they had put him in danger.

stories.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna, who asked to meet him.
stories.turn: Rav Huna saw he wore no head covering, and Rav Hamnuna explained he was unmarried.
stories.outcome: Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to see his face until he married.
stories.summary: Rav Hisda kept praising Rav Hamnuna as a great man, and Rav Huna asked to meet him. When he came without the scholar's head cloth and explained it was because he was not married, Rav Huna turned away and told him not to come back into his sight until he had married.
